content: The suppliers and distributors operating in Hubei province, China, appear to be highly context-specific. The issue being addressed involves the potential overcrowding of the marketplace with suppliers and distributors. The proposed solution involves implementing various types of consolidated contracts to increase the business volume for these entities. This is the only study that examines the availability of medicines following pooled procurement. None of the studies identified have addressed the effects of pooled procurement on the volume, availability, or affordability of medicines, nor have they explored potential adverse outcomes associated with pooled procurement. The quality of evidence was assessed as moderate in all cases. The risk of bias was judged to be low in the majority of the evidence, with five out of six studies demonstrating low risk of bias across at least three out of four domains. According to EPOC guidelines, all observational evidence is initially assigned a low-quality score. However, strong study designs have the potential to be upgraded. All studies included in this review employed rigorous study designs and transparently reported their methods and analytical approaches, leading to a methodological quality assessment of moderate. In their 2009 study on procurement strategies, Waning et al. identified a gap in empirical evidence, noting that while some surveys and desk reviews have described potential pooled procurement mechanisms in developing countries, insufficient empirical research has been conducted to validate pooled procurement and identify the conditions under which it can operate most efficiently. This review confirms the lack of empirical evidence until 2012, when the first study included in this review was published. Huff-Rousselle, in her 2012 review and informant interview report, argued that the price benefits of pooled procurement may depend equally on purchasing power and the ability to make prompt payments. If participating countries fail to adhere to payment agreements, pooled procurement could potentially lead to price increases. Similarly, the author suggests that price benefits observed in prominent examples of pooled procurement, such as the PAHO Strategic Fund, may result from strong financial backing by donors or the exclusion of non-paying countries from the procurement pool. This notion is supported by one study in the present review, which suggests that the participation of less creditworthy entities in a procurement pool could indeed increase prices. A 2017 review by Seidman and Atun of procurement and supply chain interventions broadly included 11 references on centralized procurement. However, upon inspection, none of the six studies included in this review were identified in their analysis. Additionally, none of the references in their review were eligible for inclusion in the present review due to study design limitations, such as uncontrolled before/after studies and descriptive/non-quantitative analyses. Nevertheless, the authors of that review suggest that both national (centralized) and international pooled procurement have the potential to deliver cost savings across multiple settings. Although the study designs informing this conclusion are weak, the directionality of the evidence aligns with the findings of the present review. A scoping review of literature from Latin American countries by Soares et al. identified two studies on pooled purchasing. One of these studies was also covered by Seidman and Atun, while the other was not eligible for inclusion in the present review due to study design limitations. The objectives of the Soares et al. review were to examine the scope and aspects discussed in peer-reviewed papers on public procurement in South American countries. As such, their results are not directly comparable to the present review. No further reviews on this topic are known to the authors. The empirical evidence suggests that pooled procurement is likely effective in lowering prices. However, this effect may be less pronounced in highly concentrated (monopolized) markets. The benefits of pooled procurement may be more significant in settings with lower institutional quality or higher corruption and less pronounced if procurement pools include purchasers with poor payment records. Future research is needed to further substantiate these findings using robust study designs. Specifically, future work should systematically elucidate the institutional, contextual, and competitive conditions under which pooled procurement is effective in reducing prices. This is particularly relevant for regions currently working toward implementing pooled procurement, such as the East African Community, the Southern African Development Community, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Additionally, the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) may present longer-term opportunities for pooled procurement across the continent. The emergence of regional initiatives in high-income countries, such as the Beneluxa initiative, also presents valuable opportunities for learning. Value-based pricing (VBP) is defined as a policy to set prices for new medicines and/or decide on reimbursement based on the therapeutic value the medicines confer, typically assessed in the context of Health Technology Assessment (HTA). Economic analysis has been part of reimbursement decisions for the past two to three decades, with the earliest examples of this practice appearing in the early 1990s. The role of HTA bodies has been to make recommendations on the future use of new (and existing) technologies using a transparent process with a set of defined rules. The HTA process allows for a systematic assessment of the clinical and economic value of a new technology, including an evaluation of appropriate indications and the proportionality between additional costs and benefits. This, in turn, can be used to negotiate a value-based price. Although HTA and VBP are adopted in many European countries, recommendations resulting from the assessment of the same technology can differ widely across countries. While relative effectiveness evaluation is always undertaken, the scope of economic assessment (cost-effectiveness and budget impact) tends to vary, influencing the resulting recommendations. Variants of VBP and HTA are adopted in a broad range of countries, and the definitions of value and innovation tend to differ. However, some concepts, such as severity, unmet need, or rarity of illness, are commonly referred to and are often associated with a higher willingness to pay. Processes, procedures, and outcomes of assessments, including reimbursement decisions and the time taken to reach decisions, vary considerably across countries. VBP is often used in conjunction with other pricing policies, although the objectives of such policies are not always consistent. For example, external price referencing aims to set prices relative to other (similar) countries, whereas VBP is intended to set locally appropriate prices. VBP can also be considered in the context of disinvestment, using the same principles to assess the clinical and economic value of technologies that may no longer represent value for money. This can include full delisting, restricting use to specific sub-populations or indications where the technology is cost-effective, or setting prices at a level where the technology becomes cost-effective. Initially implemented in high-income settings, countries across the world, including in Asia and Latin America, are increasingly adopting VBP policies. The present section reviews the evidence on the effectiveness of VBP policies globally. Of the 10 studies assessed at the full-text level, seven were excluded. One was a review, two were commentaries with no data, and four were excluded based on study design limitations. The study designs included interrupted time series (ITS), repeated measures (RM), and panel data analysis. The interventions assessed included national procedures for disinvestment of cost-ineffective pharmaceuticals and macro-level impacts of cost-effectiveness analysis/VBP. The overall quality of evidence for price outcomes was assessed as moderate, while the evidence for expenditure outcomes was assessed as very low.
